explanations: terra: The repeated memory of Pharaoh's people slaughtering sons and sparing women sets collective child-killing against his personal boast that he raised Moses.

luna: The source section pairs عسر and يسر in childbirth. In the fasting passage God says “يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ بِكُمُ الْيُسْرَ وَلَا يُرِيدُ بِكُمُ الْعُسْرَ”; this repeats the same ease/hardship boundary in a different legal setting. | terra: يُرِيدُ ٱللَّهُ بِكُمُ ٱلْيُسْرَ وَلَا يُرِيدُ بِكُمُ ٱلْعُسْرَ states divine intent as ease rather than hardship, a direct interpretive frame for the section's paired terms.
terra: In a divorce context, women may not conceal what God created in their wombs; hidden pregnancy becomes legally consequential, preparing the more explicit delivery term in 65:4.

luna: The section places birth, breastfeeding, hardship, and ease together. This verse regulates nursing and weaning and says “لَا تُضَارَّ وَالِدَةٌ بِوَلَدِهَا,” making the child's dependence and the mother's bodily burden a concrete duty of care. | terra: Mothers nurse for two complete years, fathers provide fairly, and no soul is burdened beyond capacity; the ayah joins nursing, completion, provision, and a limit on imposed weight.
terra: Those who spend without following their gift by reproachful reminder or injury retain their reward; this supplies the positive boundary against Pharaoh's weaponized recollection of care.
terra: Believers are told not to nullify charity by reproachful reminders and injury; this names what is wrong with Pharaoh's use of remembered upbringing as leverage.
terra: A debtor in عُسْرَةٍ receives time إِلَىٰ مَيْسَرَةٍ; material constriction is answered by patient room, making ease an ethical practice rather than only a future event.

luna: The section's load is something carried and then removed. This prayer asks God “وَلَا تَحْمِلْ عَلَيْنَا إِصْرًا,” naming the opposite movement: do not impose a heavy burden on us. | terra: The prayer asks the Rabb not to تَحْمِلْ عَلَيْنَا إِصْرًا or load people beyond their power, converting heavy-load language into an appeal for merciful measure and relief.

luna: The section moves from pregnancy to a child being received and raised. This ayah says God forms people in wombs “كَيْفَ يَشَاءُ,” connecting the sexed birth scene to divine knowledge and formation before birth. | terra: God forms people in the wombs however He wills; the hidden child is shaped under divine choice before any human valuation as male or female.
terra: The family of Imran is introduced as offspring, one from another, just before the pregnant woman's vow; the birth scene thus belongs to a continuing but divinely heard lineage.

luna: The section says Imran's wife dedicated what was in her womb; this preceding verse gives her vow, “مَا فِي بَطْنِي مُحَرَّرًا.” It supplies why the sex of the child matters in the next ayah, 3:36. | terra: Before the delivery in 3:36, Imran's wife dedicates مَا فِي بَطْنِي and asks God to accept it; the unborn child is already carried, entrusted, and oriented toward divine reception.

luna: The source section labels ذ ك ر's dictionary sense as a male child and recalls the old birth formula “أيسرت وأذكرت.” Mary instead says “وَضَعْتُهَا أُنثَىٰ,” then the verse distinguishes الذكر from الأنثى; the scene lets the reader hear that inherited ranking beside this particular birth. | terra: Imran's wife says وَضَعَتْهَا and وَضَعْتُهَا أُنثَىٰ: the section's unloading/birth sense of وضع is enacted, while the girl's reception challenges the old formula that coupled easy birth with a boy.

luna: The source section connects ربّ (root ر ب ب) with staged nurturing and a caregiver. Here her Lord “وَأَنبَتَهَا نَبَاتًا حَسَنًا” and entrusts her to Zakariyya, showing the girl welcomed and raised well after the old formula had treated a male birth as the favorable outcome. | terra: After the girl's birth in 3:36, her Rabb accepts her well, causes her to grow وَأَنۢبَتَهَا نَبَاتًا حَسَنًا, and entrusts her to Zechariah; this gathers divine nurture, gradual growth, and human caregiving around the child whom the old curse devalued.

luna: Immediately after the section's scene of Mary being accepted and raised, Zakariyya asks his Lord for good offspring. This ayah's own contribution is the request for a child after he witnesses Mary's provision; it extends the birth-and-care scene into a prayer for offspring. | terra: Immediately after seeing Mary's divinely supplied nurture in 3:37, Zechariah asks his Rabb for ذُرِّيَّةً طَيِّبَةً, so caregiving awakens a prayer for offspring rather than a preference for one sex.

luna: Continuing Zakariyya's request in 3:38, this ayah announces Yahya to him. Its own contribution is the promised male child, carrying the section's childbearing scene and male-child wording forward into the next moment of the same passage. | terra: The angels announce Yahya to Zechariah while he stands praying, supplying the promised child immediately after his prayer awakened by Mary's care and provision.

luna: This ayah has Zakariyya ask how he could have a boy in old age when his wife is barren. It completes the childbearing difficulty behind the announcement in 3:39, giving the section's hardship/ease and male-birth details a concrete fertility parallel. | terra: Zechariah asks how he can have a boy in old age with a barren wife; bodily impossibility makes the child a gift of divine agency rather than the reward presumed by a birth formula.

terra: After the promised boy, Zechariah is told وَٱذْكُر رَّبَّكَ كَثِيرًا; the passage places Qur'anic remembrance beside male offspring and thus exposes the distinct senses gathered under the section's ذكر root.
terra: The girl accepted and grown in 3:36–37 is later told that God chose and purified her above the women of the worlds, a decisive reversal of the inherited shame attached to a female birth.
terra: The casting of pens asks أَيُّهُمْ يَكْفُلُ مَرْيَمَ, recalling how Mary's caregiver was chosen; it supplies the contested human guardianship behind 3:37's divine nurturing.
terra: The angels give Mary news of a child identified as the Messiah, initiating the promised-birth scene whose human impossibility she voices in 3:47.
terra: The promised child will speak in the cradle and in maturity, placing infancy and completed growth side by side within Mary's announcement scene.
terra: Mary asks her Rabb how she can have a child when no man has touched her, and the answer places the otherwise impossible birth under God's unrestricted creating and command.
terra: In the same surah as Mary's birth, God says He never wastes the work of male or female and بَعْضُكُم مِّنۢ بَعْضٍ, giving an explicit answer to gendered devaluation.
terra: Humanity comes from one soul and its mate and spreads into many men and women, while the ayah closes by invoking womb-ties; sex, reproduction, and kinship share one origin.

luna: The section develops child-rearing through its root ر ب ب and caregiver sense. This verse requires testing orphans until they reach marriageable maturity before handing over their property, a specific legal form of care through growth.

luna: The source section explicitly labels رَبِيبَة as a caregiver/child-care word from root ر ب ب. This verse names “رَبَائِبُكُمُ اللَّاتِي فِي حُجُورِكُم,” stepdaughters under one's care, giving that secondary family-and-guardianship sense a Qur'anic setting. | terra: The ayah places nursing mothers and sisters beside رَبَائِبُكُمْ, whose Qur'anic sense is stepdaughters rather than the source dictionary's “caretakers”; the same root-family neighborhood clarifies both child care and a semantic boundary.
terra: One who shifts his own offense onto an innocent person has اِحْتَمَلَ بُهْتَـٰنًا وَإِثْمًا, showing that false transfer only adds a new carried sin.
terra: Whoever does righteous deeds, male or female, while believing enters the Garden without injustice; divine acceptance is explicitly independent of the sex privileged by the old birth formula.

luna: The source section describes وِزْر as a heavy sin-load and the surah itself pictures a load weighing on the back. This verse says people carry their burdens “عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ,” making the moral weight bodily visible. | terra: The deniers يَحْمِلُونَ أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ, turning the section's definition of wizr as a heavy sin-load into a burden visibly borne on backs.

terra: The pagans reserve what is in livestock wombs for males and forbid it to wives, with another rule for stillbirth; condemned gendered claims over womb-content mirror the section's rejected valuation of sex.
terra: Livestock are described as حَمُولَةً وَفَرْشًا, burden-bearing and smaller animals, giving the section's flock vocabulary a concrete spectrum of carrying capacity.

luna: The section links the new-born sheep (dictionary form الرُّبَّى, root ر ب ب) with childbirth and also discusses male/female birth. This verse names sheep and goats, then asks about males, females, and what the females' wombs contain, joining the flock to sexed birth and human claims about it. | terra: The ayah names sheep and goats, males and females, and مَا ٱشْتَمَلَتْ عَلَيْهِ أَرْحَامُ ٱلْأُنثَيَيْنِ; it gathers the section's flock, womb, and sex distinctions while challenging invented gender rules.

luna: This neighbor continues the livestock argument from 6:143 with camels and cattle and again asks what their wombs contain. Its own contribution extends the sex-and-womb test from sheep and goats to other herd animals. | terra: The next livestock pairs again ask whether males, females, or what wombs contain were forbidden, extending 6:143's challenge to invented sex distinctions.
terra: The parallel ban on killing children because of poverty says God provides for parents and children, again defining care and provision as the answer to fear around offspring.

luna: The source section defines وِزْر as a heavy load of sin. This verse's “وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ” makes that moral burden explicit and says each bears their own. | terra: With the Rabb named at both ends, وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ fixes moral weight to its bearer; divine removal cannot be mistaken for shifting guilt to someone else.
terra: This recurrence again names the slaughter of sons and survival of women as a severe trial, preventing Pharaoh's household nurture from being read apart from its violence.

luna: The source section's word وضع describes setting down the carried burden. This verse says the Messenger “يَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ وَالْأَغْلَالَ,” a direct reversal in which burdens and shackles are removed from people. | terra: The messenger يَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ and their shackles; this is the closest external enactment of the surah's placing-off of a crushing burden.

luna: The source section describes pregnancy as a burden that is carried and eventually set down. Here the wife “حَمَلَتْ حَمْلًا خَفِيفًا” and later both parents ask for a sound child, showing pregnancy as a changing, shared human concern. | terra: The wife first حَمَلَتْ حَمْلًا خَفِيفًا, then becomes heavy and the pair pray to their Rabb for a sound child; light load, increasing weight, birth hope, and dependence converge.
terra: Abraham's wife receives news of Isaac and then Jacob while standing nearby, a birth promise that includes generational continuation.
terra: She asks أَأَلِدُ وَأَنَا۠ عَجُوزٌ with an aged husband, making bodily difficulty explicit in the voice of the prospective mother.
terra: The messengers answer that God's mercy and blessings are upon the household, locating the extraordinary birth under the Rabb's care.
terra: Joseph's buyer proposes honoring his lodging or taking him as a child, while God is establishing him in the land; human adoption becomes one instrument of hidden nurture.
terra: When Joseph reaches maturity, God gives him judgment and knowledge; the child whom a household considered adopting in 12:21 is shown brought to full capability.

luna: The section's womb-and-birth image includes what is carried and what is born. This verse says God knows what each female carries and what wombs “تَغِيضُ” or increase, giving the hidden changes of pregnancy a measure known to God. | terra: God knows مَا تَحْمِلُ كُلُّ أُنثَىٰ, what wombs diminish or increase, and gives everything a measure; it makes gestation a hidden, changing process held within exact measure.
terra: Moses himself recalls deliverance from Pharaoh's slaughter of sons, a direct counter-memory to Pharaoh's self-serving recollection in 26:18.
terra: Abraham asks whether they give him birth tidings despite old age, another concrete boundary where apparent difficulty does not prevent the promised child.
terra: Livestock provide warmth, benefits, and food, a broad but concrete picture of the useful abundance behind the section's milk-rich, fruitful flock sense.
terra: Livestock تَحْمِلُ أَثْقَالَكُمْ to a land reachable only with severe strain, while “your Rabb” is compassionate; carrying a heavy load and merciful easing occupy one concrete scene.

luna: The source section says وِزْر is the heavy load of sin. This verse says opponents will carry “أَوْزَارَهُمْ كَامِلَةً” and burdens from those they misled, giving the load a consequence that extends beyond the carrier. | terra: Those who mislead others carry their own أَوْزَارَهُمْ كَامِلَةً and part of others' burdens; the image of load is intensified by accumulation rather than relieved by transfer.

luna: Before the darkened face and threatened burial in 16:58–59, this ayah says the people assign daughters to God while reserving what they desire for themselves. Its own contribution is the gendered hierarchy that frames the section's old birth blessing favoring boys.

luna: The section sets an old preference for male birth beside the Qur'anic girl born to Imran's wife. This verse shows the contrary response to a daughter: the father's face darkens at the news, exposing the social devaluation the section's birth formula preserves. | terra: When one of them is given news of a female, his face darkens; this human reaction is the precise opposite of the Rabb's good acceptance of Mary.

luna: Continuing 16:58, this verse shows the father hiding from people and weighing humiliation against burying the child. It supplies the consequence of the darkened face, a stark reversal of the good acceptance and care in 3:37. | terra: The father hides from people and debates keeping the girl in humiliation or burying her, exposing the evil judgment behind the old female-birth curse.

luna: The source section uses flock milk as a secondary dictionary sense of ي س ر. This verse describes drinkable milk coming from livestock bellies, a specific bodily source for the abundance image rather than merely a shared word. | terra: Livestock bellies yield pure milk for drinkers, a direct Qur'anic counterpart to the source dictionary's secondary picture of a flock abundant in milk.

luna: The section follows birth into a child's care and growth. This verse says people are brought from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing, then given hearing, sight, and hearts; its contribution is the newborn's beginning and subsequent capacity. | terra: God brings people from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing and gives hearing, sight, and hearts; birth opens into the faculties by which a dependent child is gradually made capable.
terra: In the same surah that depicts shame at a daughter's announcement, God promises a good life and full reward to any believing doer of good, male or female.

luna: The source section labels the surah's وِزْر as a heavy sin-load. This verse says “وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ,” specifying the moral boundary on who can bear such a load. | terra: وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ repeats the non-transfer rule and ties accountability to receiving a messenger, sharpening what kind of load the section's wizr is.

luna: The source section's dictionary form التربية (root ر ب ب) describes raising step by step. This prayer asks mercy for parents “كَمَا رَبَّيَانِي صَغِيرًا,” naming childhood care as a debt answered with care. | terra: رَبِّ ٱرْحَمْهُمَا كَمَا رَبَّيَانِي صَغِيرًا uses the Rabb root for parents' raising a small child and turns received nurture into a prayer for mercy toward the caregivers.
terra: The command not to kill children from fear of poverty is grounded in God's provision for them and their parents, opposing anxious destruction to Rabb-like provision after birth.

luna: The section recalls a traditional birth formula favoring male offspring. This ayah challenges the same preference in a theological reversal, asking whether God selected sons for people and took females from among the angels.
terra: God honors the children of Adam, carries them on land and sea, and provides good things; carrying and provision become acts of continuing divine care for those once carried in wombs.
terra: Moses asks that forgetfulness not be held against him and that he not be burdened with difficulty in his affair, a human plea for room inside a demanding apprenticeship.

luna: The source section's dictionary account of التربية (root ر ب ب) is gradual growth toward completion. Here the Lord protects the treasure for two orphan boys “أَن يَبْلُغَا أَشُدَّهُمَا,” tying guardianship to the children reaching maturity. | terra: The Rabb preserves two orphans' treasure until they reach full strength; this is gradual protective nurture aimed at completion, exactly the section's definition of tarbiya enacted as providence.
terra: وَسَنَقُولُ لَهُ مِنْ أَمْرِنَا يُسْرًا closely matches the promise of ease “in his affair” in 65:4, but in the setting of just rule over a believing person.

luna: In the same surah as Mary's labor scene, Zakariyya describes his failing strength and white hair before asking for a child in 19:5. This ayah contributes bodily frailty as the setting for a difficult, late-life birth request.

luna: Zakariyya asks his Lord for a successor and says his wife is barren; the following 19:7 announces a boy. This is a specific childbearing difficulty and divine provision parallel to the section's births and its movement from hardship to ease. | terra: Zechariah tells his Rabb that his wife is barren and asks for an heir, placing hoped-for birth inside acknowledged human inability.

luna: This ayah asks that the requested child inherit Zakariyya and the family of Jacob, extending the childbirth request in 19:5 into care and succession. It adds the future role of the child to the section's wordplay about a newborn and the root ر ب ب's nurturing sense.

luna: This ayah announces Yahya as a son to the aged Zakariyya and barren wife from 19:4–5. Its own contribution is the promise of a child despite those obstacles, a direct instance of ease following reproductive hardship. | terra: The answer announces a boy, Yahya, with a name not given before, presenting male offspring as a singular divine gift rather than a conventional sign of easy fortune.

luna: Zakariyya asks how he can have a boy when he is old and his wife barren. This ayah states the obstacle from his perspective; 19:9 supplies God's answer, so the row's contribution is the felt difficulty of the promised birth. | terra: Zechariah asks how a boy can come when his wife is barren and he has reached extreme old age, a repeated scene of hardship overcome by creation.

terra: When Zechariah asks how the promised boy can come, his Rabb answers that it is easy for Him and recalls creating Zechariah from nothing; divine ease directly answers apparent reproductive impossibility.
terra: Mary asks how she can have a boy when no man has touched her and she has not been unchaste; her stated obstacle gives 19:21's declaration of divine ease its concrete birth context.

terra: Mary's corresponding birth question receives the answer that it is easy for her Rabb, who will make the child a sign and mercy; this is a nonlexical but explicit promise of ease immediately before she carries him in 19:22.

luna: The source section compares a burden carried with a pregnancy carried. Mary “فَحَمَلَتْهُ” and withdraws with it, giving that comparison a concrete pregnancy scene before the labor in 19:23. | terra: فَحَمَلَتْهُ begins Mary's pregnancy and withdrawal, giving the bodily carrying that culminates in the labor of 19:23.

luna: The section explicitly recalls this birth: labor (“الْمَخَاضُ”) brings Mary to a palm trunk. The scene anchors its language of carrying and setting down in the pain of an actual delivery. | terra: Labor pains drive Mary to the palm trunk; this supplies the concrete difficult-birth scene behind the source dictionary's عسر formula rather than merely sharing a word for hardship.

luna: This neighbor to the labor in 19:23 contributes reassurance and provision: Mary is told “أَلَّا تَحْزَنِي” and that her Lord has placed a stream below her. The following 19:25 completes the immediate care with dates; this ayah supplies comfort during the birth scene. | terra: At the point of labor, a call tells Mary not to grieve and announces a stream beneath her; the birth hardship is met from within by immediate reassurance and provision.

luna: Continuing the birth scene of 19:23–24, this ayah tells Mary to shake the palm trunk so fresh dates fall (“رُطَبًا جَنِيًّا”). Its own contribution is food provided to the mother at delivery. | terra: Mary is told during labor to shake the palm so fresh dates fall; her own small action meets provision within the difficult birth scene.
terra: “Eat, drink, and be comforted” completes the immediate care after labor, making bodily replenishment part of the transition from carrying to birth.
terra: Mary returns to her people تَحْمِلُهُ, so حمل now names carrying the born child in her arms rather than carrying him in the womb, a precise shift within the same scene.

luna: Continuing Mary's delivery scene after the reassurance and dates in 19:24–26, this ayah presents the infant Jesus in the cradle while people challenge Mary. Its own contribution is the newborn and his mother's public encounter, extending the section's delivery image into infancy.
terra: God says He has made the revelation easy in the Prophet's tongue to give good news and warning, a second “We eased it for you” stance centered on communication.
terra: Moses prays رَبِّ ٱشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي just before asking for ease; the child once raised in Pharaoh's house now seeks his Rabb's opening and preparation.
terra: وَيَسِّرْ لِي أَمْرِي is Moses' direct request that his Rabb make the mission easy, linking the Pharaoh upbringing scene to divinely prepared ease.

terra: Before recounting Moses' infancy, God says that He had already favored him another time; this divine reminder of nurturing favor is the direct counterpart to Pharaoh's self-serving reminder in 26:18.
terra: God recalls inspiring Moses' mother, making maternal action itself part of the hidden divine nurture elaborated in 20:39–40.

luna: The source section connects ربّ (root ر ب ب) with nurture. God says of infant Moses “وَلِتُصْنَعَ عَلَىٰ عَيْنِي,” making divine protection through childhood a counterpart to the section's image of the Lord who raises. | terra: The infant Moses is placed where Pharaoh's household will take him, yet God says وَلِتُصْنَعَ عَلَىٰ عَيْنِي; his formation and care are claimed as divine even inside the human palace.
terra: Moses' sister finds a carer, he is returned to his mother, rescued from distress, tested through stages, and arrives عَلَىٰ قَدَرٍ; the ayah compresses nursing, relief, formation, and measure.
terra: The people say حُمِّلْنَا أَوْزَارًا of ornaments and then cast them away; a literal load is carried and unloaded, clarifying the physical metaphor inside moral وزر.
terra: God tells the same prophetic addressee that He has given him from Himself ذِكْرًا; 20:100 then makes turning from this remembrance result in carrying a wizr.

luna: The source section defines وِزْر as a weighty sin-load. This verse says one who turns away from the Reminder will carry “وِزْرًا” on the Resurrection Day, giving that secondary sense a precise judgment scene. | terra: Whoever turns from the revealed reminder فَإِنَّهُ يَحْمِلُ يَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَـٰمَةِ وِزْرًا, directly joining the section's ذكر and وزر roots through reception or refusal.

luna: The source section notes that حِمْل (load) and حَمْل (pregnancy) share written letters while meaning differs. This neighboring verse calls the judgment load “حِمْلًا,” making the lexical distinction concrete beside 20:100's وِزْرًا. | terra: The burden of 20:100 is called a terrible حِمْلًا on resurrection day, making explicit that wizr is a carried load while keeping it distinct from pregnancy.
terra: The one who carries wrongdoing fails before the Living, Sustaining One; moral wrong is again made a carried load, with divine sustaining power as its setting.
terra: Zechariah prays to his Rabb not to leave him alone, expressing need for offspring without treating a child's sex as the measure of blessing.
terra: God answers, grants Yahya, and وَأَصْلَحْنَا لَهُ زَوْجَهُ; the barren condition is made fit for birth through divine response.
terra: The parallel account says God breathed into the woman who guarded her chastity and made her and her son a sign, presenting mother and born child together under divine agency.

luna: The source section's birth dictionary form is وضع الحمل, the carried thing set down. At the Hour “وَتَضَعُ كُلُّ ذَاتِ حَمْلٍ حَمْلَهَا”; the same childbirth action becomes a sign of terror rather than ordinary relief. | terra: At the Hour every nursing mother is distracted and every pregnant one تَضَعُ كُلُّ ذَاتِ حَمْلٍ حَمْلَهَا; the ordinary release of a carried child becomes an involuntary sign of overwhelming terror.

luna: The section links pregnancy, birth, and gradual growth. This verse describes formation in the womb through stages and then being brought out as an infant, showing the transition from hidden carrying to birth. | terra: The ayah follows human formation through womb stages, appointed term, birth, and maturity, then mirrors it in dead earth swelling and growing; it expands the section's gradual nurture and plant-growth metaphor.

luna: The section connects pregnancy to a carried thing that develops before birth. This verse places the drop “فِي قَرَارٍ مَّكِينٍ,” naming the womb as a secure lodging and giving the carrying image its protected setting. | terra: The human drop is placed in قَرَارٍ مَّكِينٍ, a secure lodging, giving the carried child a protected hidden place before the stages of 23:14.

luna: The source section defines التربية (root ر ب ب) as developing something stage by stage to completion. This verse recounts the embryo's stages and its development “خَلْقًا آخَرَ,” a direct bodily counterpart to that dictionary description. | terra: Successive transformations lead to ثُمَّ أَنشَأْنَـٰهُ خَلْقًا ءَاخَرَ, a Qur'anic picture of development stage by stage toward a completed new creature.

luna: The source section's dictionary form يَسَرَتِ الْغَنَمُ (root ي س ر) describes a flock increasing in milk and offspring. This verse points to cattle, drink from their bellies, and their many benefits, giving the milk side of that livestock abundance a Qur'anic scene. | terra: The livestock lesson again gives drink from their bellies and many benefits, grounding the section's flock-abundance sense in provided nourishment.
terra: Immediately after the livestock milk and benefits of 23:21, people are carried on the animals and on ships; nourishment and burden-bearing are consecutive provisions.
terra: God makes Mary's son and his mother a sign and shelters them on secure high ground with rest and flowing water, extending the birth image into protective lodging and provision.
terra: The messenger bears what he is charged with and the audience bears what it is charged with, using carrying for assigned responsibility and preserving the distinction between burdens.

luna: The section notes the source-surah's opening question and contrasts God's reassurance with Pharaoh's reproach. Pharaoh asks “أَلَمْ نُرَبِّكَ فِينَا وَلِيدًا,” claiming to have raised Moses as an infant; the same root of nurture becomes a weapon for asserting control. | terra: Pharaoh asks أَلَمْ نُرَبِّكَ فِينَا وَلِيدًا, using the same “did we not … you” recollection as the surah while turning nurture into a boast against the person raised.

terra: Moses answers Pharaoh's claimed favor by pointing to his enslavement of the Children of Israel; the human boast of raising one child is bounded by the oppression that made that upbringing possible.
terra: Pharaoh slaughters sons and spares women while weakening a people; his later claim to have nurtured Moses is illuminated by the regime's destruction of other children.
terra: Moses' mother is told to nurse him and promised both his return and future mission, joining immediate maternal care to a hidden divine plan for the child.
terra: Pharaoh's household picks up the exposed infant who will become their enemy, beginning the paradoxical human upbringing later claimed in 26:18.
terra: Pharaoh's wife calls the infant a comfort and proposes taking him as a child; adoptive welcome inside a murderous regime complicates Pharaoh's later boast of nurture.
terra: After losing the infant, Moses' mother's heart becomes empty and God strengthens it so she can remain faithful; maternal distress is held and made firm within the caregiving sequence.
terra: Moses' mother sends his sister to follow him, supplying the family care that leads to the nursing solution in 28:12.

luna: The section places breastfeeding and a caregiver among its birth images. This verse says wet nurses had been forbidden to Moses before his sister offered a way to find a nurse, making infant feeding part of the story's care problem. | terra: After wet nurses are barred to the infant, his sister offers a household that will يَكْفُلُونَهُ and care sincerely; this is the caregiver sense made into a concrete nursing search.

luna: Continuing 28:12, this verse returns Moses to his mother “كَيْ تَقَرَّ عَيْنُهَا وَلَا تَحْزَنَ.” It completes the nursing episode with maternal reunion, linking feeding to the attachment and care after birth. | terra: God restores Moses to his mother so her eye may be comforted and she may know the promise true, turning separation into divinely arranged maternal nurture.
terra: When Moses reaches maturity and full strength, God gives him judgment and knowledge, completing the staged development begun with his nursing and return to his mother.
terra: The disbelievers offer وَلْنَحْمِلْ خَطَايَاكُمْ, but the ayah denies that they can carry any of others' sins, exposing a false promise to take away another's moral load.

luna: The source section describes a sin as a heavy thing carried. This verse says opponents will bear their own “أَثْقَالَهُمْ” and additional burdens for those they misled, showing moral weight accumulated through action. | terra: They will carry أَثْقَالَهُمْ وَأَثْقَالًا مَّعَ أَثْقَالِهِمْ, showing burdens added to burdens after 29:12 denies genuine transfer.
terra: Many creatures do not تَحْمِلُ رِزْقَهَا, yet God provides for them and for people; inability to carry one's provision becomes a reason for trust in the Provider.
terra: God creates from weakness, brings strength after weakness, then weakness and gray hair after strength; the life cycle makes gradual formation and decline explicit.

luna: The source section links load-bearing with birth; this verse describes a mother carrying her child “وَهْنًا عَلَىٰ وَهْنٍ” and then nursing/weaning him for two years. It extends the image from delivery into maternal care. | terra: A mother حَمَلَتْهُ أُمُّهُ وَهْنًا عَلَىٰ وَهْنٍ and weans over two years, extending the image from pregnancy's accumulating weakness into gradual post-birth care.
terra: Knowledge of what is in the wombs belongs to God among the hidden matters, reinforcing the section's movement from an unseen carried child to disclosed birth.
terra: Human progeny is made from an extract of lowly fluid, supplying the humble beginning for the shaping and faculties of 32:9.
terra: God proportions the human, breathes spirit, and gives hearing, sight, and hearts; the child is made fit in stages rather than merely delivered.
terra: The repeated male/female pairs end with ٱلذَّاكِرِينَ ٱللَّهَ كَثِيرًا وَٱلذَّاكِرَاتِ, joining sex distinction to the remembrance sense of ذكر while giving both equal promise.
terra: Those who harm innocent believers اِحْتَمَلُوا بُهْتَـٰنًا وَإِثْمًا مُّبِينًا, another explicit moral use of carrying a nonphysical load.
terra: The heavens, earth, and mountains refuse to carry the Trust, while the human حَمَلَهَا; moral responsibility appears as an immense offered load, not a pregnancy.

luna: The source section's dictionary verb وضع names giving birth. This verse says no female conceives or “تَضَعُ” except with God's knowledge, directly joining pregnancy, delivery, and what is hidden from human observers. | terra: No female وَمَا تَحْمِلُ مِنْ أُنثَىٰ وَلَا تَضَعُ except with God's knowledge, and measured life terms follow; carrying, delivery, hidden knowledge, and measure meet in one statement.

luna: The source section's dictionary definition of وِزْر is a heavy burden of sin. This verse repeats that no bearer carries another's burden, making the moral load distinct from the pregnancy sense of حَمْل discussed beside it. | terra: No burden-bearer bears another's burden, and even a مُثْقَلَةٌ calling for help with حِمْلِهَا transfers none of it; this sets the boundary around the surah's personally addressed burden and its removal.
terra: God says He carried their offspring in the laden ship, joining descendants, divine carrying, and a vessel already bearing a load in one rescue image.
terra: God reminds people that He created cattle for them, supplying the herds to which the drinks and benefits of 36:73 belong.
terra: The cattle are made manageable, with some serving as mounts and some as food; this gives the human use and control immediately before the herd's drinks are named.
terra: People have benefits and drinks from the herds God made for them; this corresponds to the source's milk-rich flock while making gratitude the proper response.
terra: Abraham asks his Rabb for a child among the righteous, another offspring prayer whose desired quality is righteousness rather than maleness as social prestige.
terra: God gives him news of a forbearing boy; the birth promise answers 37:100 and begins a father-child sequence of growth and testing.
terra: When the boy reaches the age of working alongside his father, the narrative marks gradual growth from promised child to capable companion.

luna: The section names ذ ك ر as a secondary dictionary sense for a male child and describes a birth blessing that favored boys. This ayah asks whether daughters belong to the Lord while the people take sons, another direct exposure of that sex hierarchy.

luna: This ayah asks whether God chose daughters over sons. Its own contribution is to name that ranking as the disputed claim, a repeated gendered reversal related to the section's old male-favoring birth formula.

luna: The source section develops birth and the growth of a child; this verse says God creates people in their mothers' wombs “خَلْقًا مِّن بَعْدِ خَلْقٍ” within three darknesses. It makes hidden, staged development perceptible. | terra: God creates people خَلْقًا مِّنۢ بَعْدِ خَلْقٍ in three womb-darknesses and also sends down livestock in pairs; staged gestation, the Rabb, and the section's flock sense meet here.

luna: The source section calls وِزْر a heavy load of sin. This verse repeats “وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ,” sharpening personal accountability beside the image of one thing carried and set down. | terra: The repeated rule that no bearer carries another's wizr stands beside return to “your Rabb,” placing individual burden inside Lordly judgment rather than human transfer.
terra: Pharaoh orders the sons of those who believe with Moses killed and their women spared, another direct exposure of the violent regime behind his claim to have raised one boy.
terra: The believer promises entry into the Garden to every believing righteous person, male or female, replacing valuation by sex with valuation by faith and action.

luna: The source section's dictionary form التربية (root ر ب ب) means development by stages to completion. This verse traces the human from a drop to an infant, maturity, and old age, spelling out that gradual passage. | terra: Creation proceeds from dust and a drop through a clot, birth as a child, maturity, and old age; this is the section's gradual bringing-to-completion across a whole life.
terra: God makes livestock for riding and eating, identifying the animals referred to when 40:80 adds benefits and being carried on them.
terra: Livestock supply benefits and desired needs, and people are carried on them and ships; provision and load-bearing meet in one scene.
terra: No fruit emerges and no female تَحْمِلُ مِنْ أُنثَىٰ وَلَا تَضَعُ except with God's knowledge, placing unseen gestation and its eventual disclosure under the same Lordly knowledge.
terra: God makes mates among humans and livestock and multiplies them thereby, joining human offspring to the section's secondary sense of flock increase.

luna: The source section describes a folk blessing that wished for an easy male birth and a curse tied to a girl. This verse says God “يَهَبُ لِمَن يَشَاءُ إِنَاثًا,” placing daughters within God's gift rather than treating them as an ill outcome. | terra: God grants females to whom He wills and males to whom He wills, naming daughters first as divine gifts and directly reversing the old blessing that treated the boy as the fortunate result.

luna: The source section names ذ ك ر as a male child in its secondary dictionary sense. This verse names both “ذُكْرَانًا وَإِنَاثًا” as gifts and also names barrenness, placing sex and fertility within God's measure rather than the old male-favoring birth formula. | terra: God may join male and female offspring or leave someone barren; sex and fertility are Lordly gifts and limits, not signs that difficult female birth is a curse.

luna: This ayah asks whether God has taken daughters from what He creates while selecting sons for the people; 43:17 then shows their face darkening at daughter-news. The present ayah supplies the male-over-female allocation that makes the next reaction intelligible.

luna: The source section recalls the birth saying that treated a male child as favorable and a girl as a curse. This verse describes a man darkening with anguish when given news of a daughter, a direct social reversal to the acceptance in 3:37. | terra: The one given news of what he attributes to the Merciful becomes dark-faced and suppresses grief; the repeated daughter-announcement scene again opposes divine gift to human shame.

terra: فَإِنَّمَا يَسَّرْنَـٰهُ بِلِسَانِكَ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَذَكَّرُونَ joins divine easing and remembering in address to the Prophet, reuniting the section's يسر and ذكر roots in their Qur'anic senses.

luna: The source section distinguishes حمل (pregnancy) from the written form حِمْل (a load). This verse says a mother “حَمَلَتْهُ” and “وَوَضَعَتْهُ كُرْهًا,” making the physical carrying and painful delivery explicit. | terra: حَمَلَتْهُ أُمُّهُ كُرْهًا وَوَضَعَتْهُ كُرْهًا states both painful carrying and painful delivery, grounding the section's lexical meeting in a mother's bodily hardship and the child's later maturation.

terra: After the mother's painful carrying and delivery and the child's growth to forty in 46:15, God accepts the adult's best deeds and overlooks faults; human maturation culminates in divine acceptance.

terra: حَتَّىٰ تَضَعَ ٱلْحَرْبُ أَوْزَارَهَا joins وضع and أوزار in the idiom “until war lays down its burdens,” sharply distinguishing war's equipment/weight from the personal sin-burden and childbirth senses.
terra: The believers are likened to a crop that sends out shoots, strengthens, thickens, and stands upright, an extended staged-growth counterpart to Mary's being grown as a good plant.
terra: God creates humanity from male and female, then makes taqwa—not sex—the measure of honor; this corrects the value judgment embedded in the old blessing and curse.

terra: People count their submission as a favor to the Prophet, but God says that guidance is His favor to them; this distinguishes reproachful human favor-claiming from a truthful divine reminder of care.
terra: The oath invokes bearers carrying a load; although the bearers' identification is interpretively disputed, the ayah contributes the exact act of carrying weight before 51:3 invokes ease.
terra: The next oath invokes those moving with ease, placing easy motion directly after load-bearing without specifying childbirth; the juxtaposition is a cautious indirect parallel to the section.
terra: The guests give Abraham news of a knowing boy, beginning the scene whose mother's barrenness is named in 51:29.
terra: His wife approaches in astonishment and calls herself عَجُوزٌ عَقِيمٌ, making age and barrenness the stated obstacle to birth.
terra: The messengers say “Thus has your Rabb said,” returning the unlikely birth to the wise, knowing Lord rather than to ordinary capacity.

luna: The section's old formula treated a male child as the favorable birth. This ayah challenges the inverse allocation of daughters to God and sons to people, exposing the unequal valuation behind that formula.

luna: The source section notes ذ ك ر as a male-child word and records a birth blessing that preferred boys. This verse asks “أَلَكُمُ الذَّكَرُ وَلَهُ الْأُنثَىٰ,” exposing the unequal allocation of male and female that underlies that preference.

luna: This neighbor concludes the question in 53:21 by calling it “قِسْمَةٌ ضِيزَىٰ,” an unfair division. It makes the gender hierarchy itself the problem, clarifying the section's contrast between inherited preference and God's raising of a girl.
terra: God knew people when they were أَجِنَّةٌ فِي بُطُونِ أُمَّهَـٰتِكُمْ, so the hidden unborn stage becomes grounds for humility rather than claims of purity or worth.

luna: The source section identifies وِزْر as a load of sin. This verse states that one bearer does not bear another's burden, a moral use of load-bearing that clarifies why the surah's burden is no pregnancy. | terra: أَلَّا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ restates the boundary as part of the scriptures of Moses and Abraham, giving the section's burden a durable moral rule.

luna: The source section labels ذ ك ر as a secondary dictionary sense for a male child and places it beside female birth. This verse names God’s creation of “الذَّكَرَ وَالْأُنثَىٰ” from the paired reproductive process, making both sexes part of the same created order. | terra: God creates the pair ٱلذَّكَرَ وَٱلْأُنثَىٰ, placing both sexes under one creative act rather than ranking the ease or worth of their births.
terra: The male–female pair of 53:45 comes مِن نُّطْفَةٍ إِذَا تُمْنَىٰ, rooting sexual distinction in one shared generative origin.
terra: وَلَقَدْ يَسَّرْنَا ٱلْقُرْءَانَ لِلذِّكْرِ makes ease serve remembrance, a direct Qur'anic meeting of the two roots that the section also brings together through birth vocabulary.
terra: The repeated وَيَسَّرْنَا ٱلْقُرْءَانَ لِلذِّكْرِ confirms that ease-for-remembrance is a refrain, not an isolated verbal coincidence.
terra: The third refrain again makes the Qur'an easy for ذكر after a warning narrative, showing remembered revelation as the offered ease.
terra: The fourth refrain completes the repeated association of تيسير with ذكر and invites an answering act of remembrance.
terra: God raises the sky and وَوَضَعَ ٱلْمِيزَانَ; raising and placing appear together, clarifying that وضع can establish something rather than unload or give birth.

terra: Against the legal fiction of calling a wife “mother,” the ayah says mothers are only ٱلَّـٰٓـِٔي وَلَدْنَهُمْ; actual giving birth defines the bodily relation, while speech cannot manufacture it.

terra: The donkey carrying books supplies a different kind of load: physical carriage without receiving or living the knowledge borne, sharpening the distinction between carrying and inward appropriation.
terra: Just before the pregnancy ruling, the God-fearing person is promised a way out; this supplies the release-pattern in which 65:4's childbirth and ease are heard.
terra: God provides from where the God-fearing person does not reckon and brings His purpose to completion, giving the provision and measure that frame 65:4's delivery rule.

luna: The source section's dictionary wording for childbirth is وَضَعَتِ الْمَرْأَةُ الْحَمْلَ; this verse says pregnant women's term ends when they “يَضَعْنَ حَمْلَهُنَّ,” then promises “يُسْرًا.” It joins the carried pregnancy, its laying down, and ease in one legal context. | terra: The pregnant women's term ends أَن يَضَعْنَ حَمْلَهُنَّ, and the same ayah promises the God-fearing person يُسْرًا in his affair, directly joining delivery of a carried load to divinely given ease.

luna: The section's dictionary discussion pairs عسر with birth and later discusses nursing. Here “وَإِن تَعَاسَرْتُمْ فَسَتُرْضِعُ لَهُ أُخْرَىٰ” makes difficulty between parents a breastfeeding problem with a practical alternative. | terra: The post-birth instruction provides housing and nursing, then says وَإِن تَعَاسَرْتُمْ another woman will nurse the child; it makes interpersonal difficulty part of the same delivery-and-care sequence as 65:4 and 65:7.

luna: The source section's root ع س ر / ي س ر concerns hardship and ease. This verse promises “بَعْدَ عُسْرٍ يُسْرًا” in a passage about provision according to means, giving the birth-and-care sequence an explicit assurance of relief. | terra: Within the birth and nursing passage, Allah limits burden to what He has given and promises سَيَجْعَلُ ٱللَّهُ بَعْدَ عُسْرٍ يُسْرًا, the clearest parallel to the section's divine promise of ease around hardship.
terra: Later in the same surah God says He has sent down to the believers ذِكْرًا, adding the remembrance root to the passage already joining pregnancy, difficulty, and ease.
terra: Mary guards her chastity, receives the breathed spirit, and confirms her Rabb's words; this compressed conception scene supplies the hidden beginning of the child later carried and born.
terra: God recalls that when the water overflowed, “We carried you” in the vessel so the rescue would become a remembrance; divine carrying leads to survival and remembered care.
terra: وَقَدْ خَلَقَكُمْ أَطْوَارًا states that people were created in stages, the most concise parallel to tarbiya as development حالًا فحالًا.
terra: وَٱللَّهُ أَنۢبَتَكُم مِّنَ ٱلْأَرْضِ نَبَاتًا applies plant-growth language to people, directly echoing Mary's good growth in 3:37.
terra: The trumpet day is called a difficult day; its unrelieved eschatological hardship sets up the explicit denial of ease in 74:10, unlike the section's promise of ease with hardship.
terra: The difficult day is “not easy” for the disbelievers, providing a precise boundary case where hardship is not accompanied by the ease promised to the addressed believer in the section.
terra: كَلَّا لَا وَزَرَ uses وزر to mean a refuge, not a carried sin-load; the identical form marks a semantic boundary that guards the section's burden reading.
terra: The human begins as a drop of emitted fluid, initiating the measured formation that reaches male and female in 75:39.
terra: The drop becomes a clot and God creates and proportions it, supplying the formative act immediately before the two sexes are named.

luna: The source section records an old birth formula that favored a male child over a girl. This verse says God made “الزَّوْجَيْنِ الذَّكَرَ وَالْأُنثَىٰ,” placing male and female together as the two forms produced from the reproductive process. | terra: After forming and proportioning the embryo, God makes مِنْهُ ٱلزَّوْجَيْنِ ٱلذَّكَرَ وَٱلْأُنثَىٰ; boy and girl are twin outcomes of the same measured making.
terra: God creates the human from a mixed drop as a test and makes him hearing and seeing; generative origin leads into fitted capacities and responsibility.
terra: The generative fluid is placed in قَرَارٍ مَّكِينٍ, portraying the womb as the secure place in which the load is held.
terra: The hidden placement lasts إِلَىٰ قَدَرٍ مَّعْلُومٍ, an appointed measure that parallels the pregnancy term ending in delivery.
terra: فَقَدَرْنَا فَنِعْمَ ٱلْقَـٰدِرُونَ attributes the gestational measure to divine determination, completing the secure-place sequence.
terra: God creates the human from a drop and فَقَدَّرَهُ, providing conception and measure as the context for the possibly birth-related easing of the way in 80:20.
terra: ثُمَّ ٱلسَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُ may include God's easing of the birth passage after the measured embryo in 80:19, though the “way” can also be read more broadly as life's or guidance's path.
terra: At the cosmic upheaval, pregnant she-camels are abandoned; the most prized near-birth animals lose their ordinary care, pairing an animal gestation scene with 22:2's disrupted pregnancy.

luna: The section's birth scene distinguishes girl from boy and questions the old curse attached to a girl. This verse brings the buried-alive girl before the judgment, reversing that valuation by making her the one who is asked. | terra: The buried infant girl is summoned and questioned, giving the devalued female child a public place in judgment that reverses her erasure at birth.

luna: Continuing the questioned buried girl of 81:8, this verse asks “بِأَيِّ ذَنبٍ قُتِلَتْ.” Its contribution is to name the killing as an injustice, the opposite of the section's old curse wishing a girl a hard birth. | terra: بِأَىِّ ذَنۢبٍ قُتِلَتْ denies that the newborn girl carried any guilt, a stark boundary between the section's sin-burden and violence inflicted on a female child.
terra: ٱلَّذِي خَلَقَكَ فَسَوَّىٰكَ فَعَدَلَكَ describes creating, proportioning, and balancing the person, a compact parallel to nurture toward fitness and completion.
terra: God composes the person in whatever form He wills, placing final form under divine choice rather than under a hierarchy of desired birth outcomes.
terra: The command to glorify the name of “your Rabb” opens the sequence that moves through creating, measuring, guiding, and easing in 87:2–8.
terra: The Rabb خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ—creates and makes fit—giving a terse formulation of the section's gradual bringing to completion.
terra: وَٱلَّذِي قَدَّرَ فَهَدَىٰ joins measure to guidance before the promise of easing in 87:8, making ease part of directed preparation.

luna: The source section explains ي س ر with ease and making something ready. God says “وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ,” presenting ease as preparation by the speaker, a close parallel to reassurance that ease accompanies hardship. | terra: وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ is a divine “We–you” promise to prepare the addressee for ease, closely matching the surah's stance of recalled care and promised facility.
terra: فَذَكِّرْ إِن نَّفَعَتِ ٱلذِّكْرَىٰ follows the promise of ease in 87:8, so facilitated mission issues in the act of reminding.

terra: The oath by the creation of ٱلذَّكَرَ وَٱلْأُنثَىٰ precedes two opposed kinds of facilitation in 92:7 and 92:10; the surah relocates ease and hardship from a child's sex to a person's moral course.
terra: Giving and God-consciousness are the first conditions preceding facilitation toward ease in 92:7, showing what that ease answers in its own passage.
terra: Affirming the best completes the positive stance before 92:7's promise, locating ease in moral response rather than in the sex of a birth.

luna: The source section's root ي س ر carries ease and facilitation. This verse promises “فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ,” so ease is a path someone is made ready for, not only a condition after a difficulty. | terra: فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ promises facilitation toward ease to the giving, God-fearing person, severing “easy” from the old preference for a male birth.
terra: Miserliness and self-sufficiency begin the contrary stance that culminates in facilitation toward hardship in 92:10.
terra: Denying the best completes the negative stance before 92:10, clarifying that its hardship answers refusal rather than bodily childbirth.

luna: The source section pairs عسر with يسر as hardship and ease, including birth phrases that reverse each other. This verse says “فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْعُسْرَىٰ,” the contrary direction to ease in 92:7 and a specific reversal of the section's ease promise. | terra: فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْعُسْرَىٰ is a deliberately paradoxical facilitation toward hardship for the miser who denies; it relocates عسر from childbirth to a chosen moral trajectory.

luna: The section explicitly compares the remembered-care question with the preceding surah. This verse asks “أَلَمْ يَجِدْكَ يَتِيمًا فَآوَىٰ”; its own contribution is God's sheltering of the orphan, a concrete memory of care behind reassurance. | terra: أَلَمْ يَجِدْكَ يَتِيمًا فَـَٔاوَىٰ recalls divine shelter in the same interrogative stance; unlike Pharaoh's reproach, the reminder places present strain inside a history of care.
terra: After sheltering the orphan in 93:6, God recalls finding the addressee in need of direction and guiding him; the remembered care advances in stages.
terra: The sequence ends by recalling need and divine enrichment, completing the shelter–guidance–provision pattern of Rabb-like nurture.
